title: Present Simple

revision.summary: Master the present simple for routines, facts, questions, negatives, frequency and third-person -s.

body_content:
Present Simple — the everyday tense

Use the present simple for routines, habits, repeated actions, facts, schedules, and things that are generally true. Think: What happens regularly?

1. Positive sentences

With I, you, we, they, use the base verb:

  • I work in Accra.
  • You study English every day.
  • We play football on Saturdays.
  • They live near the school.

With he, she, it, usually add -s:

  • He works in a bank.
  • She studies English every evening.
  • It rains a lot here.

2. The third-person -s rules

  • Most verbs: work → works, read → reads, play → plays.
  • Verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: add -es: watch → watches, go → goes, fix → fixes.
  • Consonant + y: change y → ies: study → studies, try → tries.
  • Vowel + y: keep y: play → plays, enjoy → enjoys.

3. Negative sentences

Use do not / don't with I/you/we/they and does not / doesn't with he/she/it. After doesn't, the main verb returns to its base form.

  • I don't work on Sunday.
  • They don't watch TV every night.
  • He doesn't work on Sunday. Not: doesn't works.
  • She doesn't like coffee.

4. Questions

Put Do or Does before the subject:

  • Do you speak English?
  • Do they live here?
  • Does he play football?
  • Does she study every day?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, I don't. / Yes, he does. / No, she doesn't.

5. Frequency words

Common words are always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never. They normally come before the main verb: I usually walk to work. She often reads at night. With be, the frequency word normally comes after be: He is always early.

6. Time expressions

Present simple often appears with every day, every week, on Mondays, in the morning, at weekends, once a month.

  • I exercise every morning.
  • We visit our family on Sundays.
  • She has an English class twice a week.

7. Facts and general truths

  • Water boils at 100°C.
  • The sun rises in the east.
  • Birds have wings.

Common mistakes

Watch the helper verb.
He works here. → Does he work here?
He doesn't work here.

Don't use -s after does/doesn't. The does already carries the third-person grammar.

Quick pattern

Positive: Subject + verb (+s for he/she/it).
Negative: Subject + don't/doesn't + base verb.
Question: Do/Does + subject + base verb?

title: Be: am/is/are

revision.summary: Master am, is and are for identity, jobs, location, age, feelings, descriptions, negatives and questions.

body_content:
Be: am / is / are — the verb that connects

The verb be is one of the most important English verbs. In the present tense it changes to am, is, or are. Use it to talk about identity, description, age, location, feelings, jobs, and states.

1. Choose the correct form

  • I am ready.
  • You are my friend.
  • He is a teacher.
  • She is happy.
  • It is cold.
  • We are at home.
  • They are students.

2. The core pattern

I → am
He / She / It → is
You / We / They → are

3. Contractions

  • I am → I'm
  • He is → He's
  • She is → She's
  • It is → It's
  • You are → You're
  • We are → We're
  • They are → They're

4. Uses of be

  • Identity: I am Daniel. She is my sister.
  • Job: He is a doctor. They are teachers.
  • Location: We are at school. The keys are on the table.
  • Feelings/states: I am tired. You are hungry.
  • Age: I am 20 years old. She is ten.
  • Description: The room is small. They are friendly.

5. Negative sentences

Add not after am/is/are:

  • I am not tired.
  • He is not at work.
  • She isn't angry.
  • We aren't late.
  • They aren't from Ghana.

Notice that we do not use do/does with be: She isn't happy. Not: She doesn't be happy.

6. Questions with be

Move am/is/are before the subject:

  • Am I late?
  • Is he your brother?
  • Is she at home?
  • Are you ready?
  • Are they students?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. / Yes, he is. / No, he isn't. / Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.

7. Be vs. ordinary verbs

Use be for a state or identity: She is tired. Use an ordinary verb for an action: She works every day.

  • He is a teacher. → identity/job
  • He teaches English. → action
  • They are at home. → location
  • They watch TV. → action

Common mistakes

Match the subject and be.
I am happy. ✓
She is happy. ✓
They are happy. ✓

Don't add do/does. Are you ready? ✓   Do you are ready? ✗

Quick pattern

Positive: Subject + am/is/are + complement.
Negative: Subject + am/is/are + not + complement.
Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + complement?
